I have to admit, I’m not really a fan of this game. 
It’s somewhat enjoyable for a short time, but several aspects didn’t work for me.

First, the ships on the main map are just small blue silhouettes, 
which feels underwhelming—especially compared to Civilization VI, where units are clearly detailed. 
The ships do look good during combat, but that detail doesn’t carry over to the main view.

I also ran into occasional bugs. For example, the interface sometimes indicated 
that a ship was available to move when there wasn’t one. 
It wasn’t game-breaking, but it was annoying—restarting the game seemed to fix it.

The tech tree is very large and filled with explanations, but the heavy sci-fi terminology 
makes it hard to connect with. In Civilization, research feels intuitive and grounded in real history, 
but here the concepts are so abstract that they become difficult to follow. 
I found myself reading long descriptions that ultimately felt meaningless.

The map itself also feels quite empty. While I understand that space is the setting, 
it still comes across as lacking substance unless you’re really into this kind of theme.

There are also some localization issues. When playing in German, certain words didn’t fit 
properly in the UI and were awkwardly split across lines, which hurt the overall presentation (this was on a 1080p resolution).

Additionally, the number of quests, events, and technical descriptions can feel overwhelming. 
It’s hard to keep track of what’s going on or what I should focus on.

The tech tree layout is another weak point for me. 
I would have preferred a simpler tab-based system with a clear left-to-right progression. 
The current circular design requires a lot of navigation, and I often ended up 
just selecting a suggested technology without fully understanding it.

Overall, I think fans of sci-fi strategy games might enjoy this more. 
But if you’re not deeply into the genre, it may be hard to get immersed.

That said, the artistic side of the game is impressive. 
The factions, colors, and overall visual style are well done.

I plan to give it another try to see if my opinion changes. 
Right now, even on the easiest difficulty, I struggle because I’m unsure what to research 
or build due to the unclear descriptions. For instance, I thought I had unlocked “Behemoth” hulls, 
but I couldn’t find them in the ship design menu.

At the moment, I’d say: Civilization is still the better experience for me.

A Gorgeous, Asymmetrical 4X Masterpiece (With a Few Black Holes)

If you are a fan of 4X strategy games like Civilization or Stellaris, Endless Space 2 offers an incredibly stylish and atmospheric alternative. Amplitude Studios managed to create a sci-fi universe that feels remarkably alive, though it isn't without its technical and mechanical quirks. 

To give an unbiased look at what works and what holds it back:

THE GOOD:
- Wildly Unique Factions: This is where the game truly shines. You aren't just playing the same empire with a simple 10% bonus to research. Every faction plays fundamentally differently. The Vodyani are religious space-vampires who live on massive arks, while the Unfallen are giant space-trees that expand their empire by growing literal vines between star systems.
- The Best UI in Strategy Gaming: Endless Space 2 is downright beautiful. The user interface is sleek, artistic, and incredibly functional. It presents a massive amount of complex data in a way that is easy to read and satisfying to interact with. 
- Deep Internal Politics: Unlike many 4X games where your population is just a static happiness meter, here, your empire's internal politics are chaotic and alive. Your citizens will form political parties, protest, and vote for laws based on the events happening in your galaxy. 
- Stunning Presentation: The cinematic battles are a joy to watch, and the ambient, soaring soundtrack is easily one of the best in the genre. 

THE BAD:
- Hands-Off Combat: If you want deep, tactical fleet command, you will be disappointed. Combat consists of assigning a basic tactic and then watching a cinematic simulation play out. It looks great, but your actual strategic input is very shallow.
- End-Game Bugs & Jank: The game suffers from some notorious late-game performance issues. You might run into the dreaded "pending turn" bug where the AI gets stuck calculating, bringing your campaign to a halt. 
- DLC Bloat: While the base game is fantastic, some of the later DLCs add convoluted systems (like hacking) that feel more like annoying chores than fun mechanics.

THE VERDICT:
Endless Space 2 is an absolute must-play for 4X fans who value atmosphere, narrative, and incredibly distinct faction mechanics. It is heavily focused on economy, politics, and exploration rather than deep military tactics. As long as you don't mind a hands-off combat system and the occasional late-game bug, you can easily sink hundreds of hours into painting this gorgeous galaxy in your colors. I highly recommend it.

Endless Space 2 is a space 4X game that follows the well-trodden classics like Master of Orion 1/2 and Stellaris. You explore space, colonise, terraform and develop planets, conduct space diplomacy, build battle fleets, and eventually take over your rivals' empires. Compared with its competitors, ES2 is rather more focused on story-driven single-player campaigns. It comes with 8 pre-written factions (and 4 more as DLC), which avoid most of the usual space opera cliches, except for the fascistic human space empire and the obvious Klingon stand-ins who use honour as a resource. There are many flavour events and quests to undertake, depending on the faction and political party in power, which provide motivation to the gameplay. Even if you have already played through the game with one faction, changing to a different faction can provide a completely different experience.

The planetary economy management is fairly standard - build buildings, grow your population, then specialise each planet to either industry, dust (money), science, or influence (diplomacy points). It lacks the population optimisation that makes Stellaris so deep. Overpopulation is a constant problem for most factions, since the carrying capacity of most planets is low and food is generally abundant. The player can only control a finite number of systems before they face large-scale revolts, which means systems with a small number of planets are practically useless unless they have some special resource. I found the late game kicks off early, as you are forced to go for a win because you can't expand anymore. Usually, this just means creating a stealth invasion fleet and making a surprise landing on the home planet of your rival empire. A lot less epic than Stellaris' end-game crises.

The diplomacy system uses influence points for taking actions and claiming non-colonizable systems like neutron stars, black holes, etc., that provide small benefits. They also block the enemy from passing through your zone of control if you close your borders to them. This helps mitigate the common problem of 4X games where the AI sneaks into your core territory and plops out a colony out of nowhere. Even though the AI are pretty passive, you will usually end up in a war at some point. The space battles have the usual tensions — long vs short-range weapons, kinetic vs energy weapons, battleships vs carriers, behemoths vs zerg fleets, etc. The battles are cinematic — you pick your strategy from a list, then watch ships shoot it up. It's fun to watch for the first few battles, after which you will just automatically skip to the results. It's also not particularly easy to understand what happened and why you lost. The shipbuilding itself is very deep and rewarding.

ES2 doesn't do anything particularly poorly and provides some interesting ideas in a well-polished package. If you need a more modern take on Master of Orion 2 or are bored with Stellaris, give this one a shot.

As someone that has spent a significant amount of time with the Civilization series and other 4X turn based and real time strategy games - Endless Space 2 can be enjoyable without the last 2 DLCs and with community patches; 

on a side note, Humankind is the worst turn based 4X I have ever played. Zero innovation and just "make number bigger" gameplay. However, the flavor text, drawings, and art style carry Endless Space on their own despite the "make number bigger" gameplay. 

It may be creatively bankrupt in terms of gameplay mechanics, but at least it is fun to look at while playing.

Want to play online? Be ready to desynch every 5 turns.

Whatever soul this franchise had left was celebrated by Sseth on YT.
